packs.title: Find the claim behind the facts
packs.subtitle: Separate what someone wants you to accept from the reasons they offer.
packs.format: Individual writing, pairs, and class discussion
objectives: Identify the main claim without strengthening it.
Distinguish a claim from supporting evidence and background.
Explain a sentence's role using its connection to the proposed action.
materials: One student handout per learner, or display the activities and use paper.
Pens or pencils; no student devices required.
Instructor guide with model answers, kept separate from the handout.
preparation: Read the three short scenarios and model answers.
Print the three-page handout double-sided if convenient, or display one activity at a time.
Tell learners that all scenarios are invented for reasoning practice; identifying a claim does not mean accepting it.

vocabulary.definition: A statement someone asks an audience to accept. In these activities, the main claim is a proposed action.
Information offered to support a claim.
Context that helps describe the situation but is not itself offered as the main support.

timeline.title: Notice the proposed action
timeline.instructions: Read the warm-up aloud. Learners write the proposed action and its reason, then compare with a partner. Use the vocabulary to name the distinction.

timeline.title: Label the library argument
timeline.instructions: Learners complete the main activity individually, then compare labels in pairs. Ask them to explain the role of the visit count rather than vote on the library policy.

timeline.title: Discuss and check
timeline.instructions: Reveal the main model answer. Use the discussion prompts to distinguish identifying the proposal from evaluating it. Correct labels by asking which sentence the other facts are meant to support.

timeline.title: Check independent understanding
timeline.instructions: Learners complete the exit ticket without their partner. Check it against the three assessment criteria before revealing the answer.

warmup.title: The bicycle rack proposal
warmup.scenario: Invented scenario: A student says, 'Six bicycles were left against classroom walls today because the rack was full. The school should add another bicycle rack.'
warmup.output: Write two labelled sentences: one for the proposed action and one for its supporting reason.
steps: Copy the action the student wants the school to take.
Copy the fact offered to support that action.
warmup.check: Does your proposed action say what the school should do, while your reason describes what happened?
warmup.modelAnswer: Proposed action: the school should add another bicycle rack. Supporting reason: six bicycles were left against classroom walls because the existing rack was full.
warmup.whyAdequate: The answer distinguishes a recommendation from the observation offered to support it. It does not claim that this is necessarily the best solution.

activity.title: The library's later closing time
activity.scenario: Invented scenario: A student writes, 'Our library closes at 5 p.m. During a four-week trial of closing at 7 p.m., weekly visits rose from 400 to 460. The council should keep the later closing time.'
activity.output: Write three labelled statements (claim, evidence, background) and one sentence explaining your labels.
steps: Copy the main claim: the proposal the writer wants the council to accept.
Copy the supporting evidence and label the remaining sentence as background.
Write one sentence explaining why the visit count is not itself the main claim.
activity.check: Have you separated the proposed action from the fact used to support it? Do not add 'always' or claim that the trial proves the policy works everywhere.
activity.modelAnswer: Claim: the council should keep the later closing time. Evidence: weekly visits rose from 400 to 460 during the trial. Background: the library normally closes at 5 p.m. The count supports the proposal; it is not the proposed action.
activity.whyAdequate: The answer names the roles of all three sentences without strengthening what the writer said. The rise in visits is relevant to the recommendation, but identifying its role does not establish that later closing caused the rise or outweighs the costs.

exitTicket.title: The community garden proposal
exitTicket.scenario: Invented scenario: A resident writes, 'The community garden opened in 2019. All 20 planting plots are in use, and 12 residents are waiting for a plot. The council should create ten more plots.'
exitTicket.output: Write the claim, evidence, and background with labels; add one sentence explaining how the evidence relates to the claim.
steps: Copy the proposed action exactly, including the number of additional plots.
Identify the fact offered in support and the fact supplying background.
Explain why the demand for plots is evidence for the proposal rather than the proposal itself.
exitTicket.check: Have you kept the proposal at ten more plots and avoided adding a guarantee that everyone will receive one?
exitTicket.modelAnswer: Claim: the council should create ten more plots. Evidence: all 20 plots are in use and 12 residents are waiting. Background: the garden opened in 2019. The demand is offered as a reason to expand; it does not itself state what the council should do.
exitTicket.whyAdequate: The answer preserves the exact proposal, identifies the supporting observation, and explains its role. It does not turn identifying a claim into proving that the proposal is sufficient or affordable.

discussion.prompt: Could someone identify the library claim correctly and still disagree with it?
discussion.guidance: Yes. Identifying a recommendation and judging its merits are different tasks. Costs, staffing, or alternative explanations could matter when evaluating it, but they are not supplied here.

discussion.prompt: Why is the sentence with the most numbers not automatically the main claim?
discussion.guidance: A sentence's role depends on what it supports, not on its length, detail, or numerical content.

misconceptions.misconception: A claim must be false or unsupported.
misconceptions.response: A claim is something proposed for acceptance. It may be true, false, well supported, or poorly supported.

misconceptions.misconception: Evidence can never itself be a claim.
misconceptions.response: An evidence statement can be a claim in another argument. Here we identify its role in supporting this main recommendation.

misconceptions.misconception: Finding the main claim proves the recommendation is good.
misconceptions.response: First identify what is being proposed; then evaluate the evidence and other relevant considerations.

adaptations.label: More support
adaptations.instructions: Read each scenario aloud and provide three labels to place beside the sentences: proposed action, supporting fact, background. Ask learners to explain one placement orally before writing.

adaptations.label: More challenge
adaptations.instructions: After the exit ticket, ask: 'Would changing the proposal from ten more plots to one hundred change the role of the demand figures, their strength as support, or both?' Expected response: their role stays evidence, but the stronger expansion proposal requires more justification.

assessmentCriteria: The proposed action is identified accurately without exaggeration.
Evidence and background are correctly distinguished.
The explanation connects the supporting fact to the proposal rather than merely repeating both.

packs.title: What does 'better' actually mean?
packs.subtitle: Turn a vague judgment into a clear rule that another person can apply.
packs.prerequisites: None; learners compare simple counts and averages without doing arithmetic.
packs.format: Individual writing, pairs, and class discussion
objectives: Identify an ambiguous term that affects a judgment.
Define the term with a measure, direction, group, and comparison period.
Apply two definitions to the same facts and explain why they yield different judgments.
materials: One student handout per learner, or display the activities and use paper.
Pens or pencils; no calculator or student device required.
Instructor guide with model answers, kept separate from the handout.
preparation: Read the scenarios and note that every before-and-after comparison uses the same stated group.
Print the three-page handout or display each activity in turn.
Explain that all figures are invented for practice, and that observing a change does not show what caused it.

vocabulary.definition: A word or phrase with more than one reasonable meaning in its context.
An observable quantity used to judge a particular feature, such as weekly interruptions or average test scores.
The times being compared, such as the four weeks before and after a rule.

timeline.title: Spot the ambiguous word
timeline.instructions: Learners complete the warm-up and compare answers. Explain that a useful definition says what is measured, what change counts as improvement, and which group and periods are compared.

timeline.title: Apply two definitions
timeline.instructions: Pairs complete the phone-rule activity. Ask them to write definitions before stating whether either measure improves. Circulate and check that both periods and the same classes are named.

timeline.title: Discuss the choice of measure
timeline.instructions: Reveal and discuss the main model answer. Use both discussion prompts. Emphasize that a purpose should guide the choice of measure and that these figures do not isolate the rule's causal effect.

timeline.title: Transfer the skill
timeline.instructions: Learners complete the bus-service exit ticket independently. Use the criteria to check their two definitions and conclusions, then discuss the model answer.

warmup.title: A more successful reading club
warmup.scenario: Invented scenario: A club leader says, 'Our reading club became more successful this month.' Average attendance per meeting rose from 12 last month to 18 this month, but the average number of books finished per member stayed at one per month.
warmup.output: Write one ambiguous phrase, two possible meanings, and the result under each meaning.
steps: Identify the phrase that needs a clearer meaning.
Give one meaning using attendance and one using books finished per member.
State whether each meaning shows improvement in this month compared with last month.
warmup.check: Do your two meanings refer to different outcomes, and does each conclusion match the figures?
warmup.modelAnswer: 'More successful' needs clarification. If it means higher average attendance per meeting this month than last month, there is improvement from 12 to 18. If it means more books finished per member per month, there is no improvement: the average remains one.
warmup.whyAdequate: The answer makes two plausible interpretations explicit and applies the supplied values. It does not assume that attendance and reading volume are interchangeable.

activity.title: Does the phone rule make lessons better?
activity.scenario: Invented scenario: A principal says a new phone rule makes lessons 'better'. In the same ten classes, weekly phone interruptions fell from 20 to 12, but average test scores stayed at 70 out of 100. Both figures compare the four weeks before the rule with the four weeks after it.
activity.output: Write two definitions, two conclusions applying those definitions, and one sentence explaining how to choose a measure.
steps: Write two possible definitions of 'better': one using interruptions and one using test scores. For each, state the direction of improvement, the group, and the comparison period.
Apply each definition to the supplied figures and say whether it shows an improvement.
Finish with one sentence explaining why the school's purpose should guide its choice of measure before results are inspected.
activity.check: Could a reader apply your two rules to the figures without guessing? Separate observing a change from claiming the rule caused it.
activity.modelAnswer: Definition 1: fewer weekly phone interruptions across these ten classes in the four weeks after the rule than before it. This measure improves from 20 to 12. Definition 2: a higher average test score in the same classes and periods. This measure shows no improvement: 70 in both periods. The school should choose according to whether its purpose is reducing disruption or improving test performance, rather than picking whichever result looks best.
activity.whyAdequate: Both definitions specify an observable measure, direction, group, and comparison. The conclusions follow from those definitions. The answer does not claim that the rule caused the observed reduction in interruptions.

exitTicket.title: A better bus service?
exitTicket.scenario: Invented scenario: A town calls its revised bus service 'better'. On the same route, average passenger waiting time fell from 12 minutes in the month before the revision to 8 minutes in the month after it. The fare per journey rose from $2 to $3 over the same comparison. No other outcomes are supplied.
exitTicket.output: Write two clear definitions of 'better', apply each to the figures, and write one sentence about choosing between them.
steps: Define 'better' using waiting time, naming the direction of improvement, route, and periods.
Define 'better' using fare per journey, again naming the direction of improvement and comparison.
State what each definition shows and why the town should identify its priority before selecting a definition.
exitTicket.check: Have you distinguished an improvement in waiting time from a worsening in affordability, without claiming either captures every aspect of the service?
exitTicket.modelAnswer: Using time: better means a lower average waiting time on this route in the month after the revision than before it. This improves from 12 to 8 minutes. Using cost: better means a lower fare per journey on the same route over those periods. This worsens because the fare rises from $2 to $3. The town should state whether it prioritizes shorter waits, lower fares, or an explicit balance before choosing its standard.
exitTicket.whyAdequate: Both rules can be applied without guessing. They lead to different judgments about different features, so an overall verdict requires a stated priority or tradeoff rather than silently changing the definition.

discussion.prompt: Are both definitions of 'better lessons' legitimate?
discussion.guidance: Both can measure relevant educational aims, but neither captures every aim. A definition must fit the purpose; usefulness does not follow merely from being easy to count.

discussion.prompt: Why choose the measure before looking at the result?
discussion.guidance: Choosing only a favorable outcome afterward can conceal disappointing results. Stating the aim and measure first makes the evaluation more transparent.

misconceptions.misconception: A precise definition is automatically the right definition.
misconceptions.response: A rule can be precise yet poorly matched to the purpose. Ask what the activity is supposed to achieve.

misconceptions.misconception: One improving measure proves the whole policy is successful.
misconceptions.response: State exactly which feature improved and consider other relevant aims before giving an overall verdict.

misconceptions.misconception: A before-and-after difference proves the rule caused it.
misconceptions.response: These exercises identify what changed under a definition. Other changes could explain the difference; no causal comparison is supplied.

adaptations.label: More support
adaptations.instructions: Use the sentence frame: 'Better means [higher/lower] [measure] for [group] in [later period] compared with [earlier period].' Let pairs explain their definitions orally before writing.

adaptations.label: More challenge
adaptations.instructions: Ask learners to describe an aim that the two phone-rule measures miss, such as student well-being, and a possible way to measure it. Accept it as a proposed measure; no conclusion about its result is justified without data.

assessmentCriteria: Each definition names a measure, direction, group, and comparison period.
The conclusions correctly apply the supplied figures to those definitions.
The explanation links the choice of measure to an aim and avoids claiming that the figures prove causation.

articleLinks.title: Define Your Terms Before You Draw Conclusions

packs.title: Which evidence deserves more weight?
packs.subtitle: Compare how evidence was gathered before deciding how much it supports a claim.
packs.prerequisites: None; all research terms are explained and no calculations are required.
packs.format: Individual writing, pairs, and class discussion
objectives: Compare evidence using participants, comparison groups, and outcome measures.
Explain why a method strengthens support without treating it as a guarantee.
State a relevant limit on transferring a result to another setting.
materials: One student handout per learner, or display the activities and use paper.
Pens or pencils; no student devices or calculator required.
Instructor guide with model answers, kept separate from the handout.
preparation: Read the vocabulary and the supplied report descriptions.
Print the three-page handout or display the activities in turn.
Explain that all reports and figures are invented. Learners should judge the described evidence, without inventing missing study details.

vocabulary.definition: A person's report of their own experience; it may be sincere without showing what caused the experience.
A group used to judge what happens under a different condition, such as usual support instead of tutoring.
Using chance to allocate participants to groups. It reduces systematic group differences on average; it does not guarantee perfectly identical groups.
The recorded result used to evaluate a claim, such as passing the same algebra exam.

timeline.title: Separate experience from a comparison
timeline.instructions: Learners complete the flashcard warm-up. Introduce testimonial and comparison group, using the model answer to explain why a second group helps.

timeline.title: Compare the tutoring reports
timeline.instructions: Pairs complete the main activity. Explain random assignment and outcome measure. Ask them to connect every reason to a stated feature, not simply say the report is scientific.

timeline.title: Discuss strength and limits
timeline.instructions: Compare pair responses with the model. Use both discussion prompts and correct the idea that sample size alone establishes cause or that one favorable study applies everywhere.

timeline.title: Assess a new comparison
timeline.instructions: Learners complete the spelling exit ticket independently. Check their reasons and limitation against the assessment criteria, then reveal the answer.

warmup.title: Do flashcards help?
warmup.scenario: Invented scenario: A tutor claims flashcards improve vocabulary test scores. Report A quotes one learner: 'It really helped me.' Report B compares two groups of 20 learners with similar starting scores, but no random assignment: flashcards versus usual review sheets. Both groups review for the same time and take the same test. All scores are reported; the flashcard group has the higher average.
warmup.output: Write three sentences: choose a report, explain one strength in how its evidence was gathered, and name one remaining uncertainty.
steps: Choose which report gives stronger evidence for the tutor's claim.
Explain how either its comparison group or common test helps assess the claim.
State one reason the description does not establish the method's effect with certainty.
warmup.check: Can you explain your choice without treating a sincere testimonial as proof or treating a comparison as a guarantee?
warmup.modelAnswer: Report B gives stronger evidence. Its common test compares the claimed outcome after two review methods with equal review time. Because learners were not randomly assigned, differences such as motivation could still partly explain the higher average; the scenario does not tell us whether that happened.
warmup.whyAdequate: The answer identifies a relevant design advantage and distinguishes an untested possible explanation from an established fact. A testimonial may describe a real experience but does not supply the same comparison.

activity.title: Two reports about algebra tutoring
activity.scenario: Invented scenario: A tutoring program claims it raises algebra pass rates. Report A quotes one volunteer saying tutoring helped. Report B follows 200 students randomly assigned to receive tutoring or usual support, uses the same exam, and reports all results: 70 of 100 tutored students pass, versus 55 of 100 others. Both reports are accurately described; use only these facts.
activity.output: Write a choice, three reasons about the method, and one question about applying the result to another school.
steps: Choose the stronger evidence for the program's claim.
Give three reasons using the number of students, the comparison groups, and the outcome measure.
State one limit: what would you still want to know before assuming the result applies to another school?
activity.check: Explain the evidence's method rather than treating a confident testimonial or a large number alone as decisive.
activity.modelAnswer: Report B is stronger: it includes 200 students rather than one selected volunteer, random assignment supplies a fairer comparison, and a common exam measures the stated outcome. I would check whether another school's students and tutoring program are similar before transferring the conclusion.
activity.whyAdequate: The answer connects three stated design features to the claim and keeps a local result separate from a universal promise. Random assignment makes it easier to judge whether tutoring caused the difference, but the description does not justify certainty about every student or setting.

exitTicket.title: Testing a spelling program
exitTicket.scenario: Invented scenario: A school claims its new spelling program improves spelling test scores. Report A quotes one parent saying the program worked for their child. Report B records 80 pupils randomly assigned to the new program or usual spelling lessons for six weeks. Both groups receive equal lesson time and take the same final test; all results are reported. The new-program group's average is 16 out of 20, compared with 13 out of 20 for the usual-lessons group. No information about other schools is supplied.
exitTicket.output: Write the stronger report, three reasons tied to its method, and one question to ask before using the result in another school.
steps: Choose the stronger report for the stated claim.
Explain how the participants, comparison groups, and common outcome measure affect the strength of the evidence.
State a relevant detail you would check before assuming another school's pupils would benefit similarly.
exitTicket.check: Have you explained the method, kept your conclusion about the reported comparison, and avoided inventing a result for another school?
exitTicket.modelAnswer: Report B is stronger. It includes 80 pupils rather than a selected parent's single experience; chance assignment and equal lesson time make the new program and usual lessons a fairer comparison; and the same final test measures the claimed outcome. Before applying the result elsewhere, I would check whether pupils' starting spelling skills and the way the program is delivered are similar. The reported higher average does not show that every pupil improved or that every school would get the same result.
exitTicket.whyAdequate: The answer connects the described methods to the claim, identifies a relevant transfer question, and states limits without dismissing the evidence or pretending the limits have already been resolved.

discussion.prompt: Why is '200 students' not enough by itself to make the tutoring evidence strong?
discussion.guidance: A large group can still be badly selected or measured. The comparison, random assignment, common exam, and complete reporting also matter.

discussion.prompt: Does stronger evidence make the testimonial worthless or prove that every tutored student benefits?
discussion.guidance: No. A testimonial can suggest questions or report experience, but is weaker for estimating a program's effect. Group results also do not establish an identical effect on every individual.

misconceptions.misconception: A bigger sample automatically proves cause.
misconceptions.response: Ask how the groups were formed and what was measured. More observations do not repair every weakness in a method.

misconceptions.misconception: Random assignment means participants were randomly chosen from everyone.
misconceptions.response: Assignment concerns allocation to groups after participation; recruitment concerns who enters the study. The scenario does not describe recruitment.

misconceptions.misconception: A higher group average means every learner improved.
misconceptions.response: An average summarizes a group. Individuals may have different outcomes; do not infer all individual changes from the mean.

adaptations.label: More support
adaptations.instructions: Use three headings for reasons: Who was included? What was compared? What was measured? Read each report aloud and have pairs locate the matching facts before explaining them.

adaptations.label: More challenge
adaptations.instructions: Ask: 'If both spelling groups used different final tests, what would become harder to interpret?' Expected response: the score difference could reflect test difficulty rather than the teaching method; scores would no longer provide the stated common measure.

assessmentCriteria: The stronger report is chosen with three reasons tied to stated methods.
The explanation goes beyond sample size and addresses comparison and measurement.
A relevant question about transferring the result is supplied without claiming certainty, universal benefit, or invented facts.
